title: Dan Klein - Superintelligence vs Super Reliability

segments.text: DAN KLEIN: Hi, everybody.
I'm Dan Klein.
I'm a professor here at UC Berkeley.
I am also the CTO at Scaled Cognition, which
is a lab focused on high-reliability agentic models
with verifiable behavior.
Let me start out by telling you a story you probably
already know, which is, due to all these amazing capabilities
of AI today, it seems like a small team, or even
a single engineer, can whip up an eye-popping demo seemingly
overnight.
Executives get really excited.
This is the future, and go, go, go.
Three months later, there are still some details to iron out.
Six months later, we're working through some reliability issues.
So will this thing ever ship?
So if you've seen something like this play out, you're not alone.
There are a bunch of studies that show that most agentic AI
initiatives and enterprises stall or fail,
and when they ship, sometimes they
can faceplant even spectacularly.
So what's going on?
What really is behind this contrast
between demos, which are easier than ever,
and that last mile to a reliable product, which
still seems to be very hard?
So really, at the core, intelligence is multifaceted.
And although systems are getting smarter and smarter,
not all aspects of intelligence are advancing at the same rate.
The key reason why it's so hard to make reliable products even
still is that reliability has not
kept pace with other aspects of intelligence.
So what does that actually mean?
Well, if you look at today's models
and you look at things like their breadth of knowledge
or their plasticity of behavior or their fluency of output,
on these axes, things are just through the roof and only
getting better.
But if you look at things like the ability
to exert precise verifiable control or the ability
to explain the output of a model,
these aspects have consistently lagged behind the others.
What does this have to do with demos versus products?
Well, to make a demo you really need the things on the left,
but if you want to be able to ship a reliable product,
suddenly everything on the right becomes critical as well.
So this kind of signature of strengths and weaknesses
both explains why it's so hard to go that last mile.
And when systems do ship, their failure modes
often encode this exact same signature
of strengths and weaknesses.
So what does that mean?
Let me give you some examples.
So maybe you've seen the burrito bot,
which is happy to take your order or debug your code.
What's going on here?
Well, this is actually the breadth
of the underlying model showing up as a flaw,
especially when accompanied by imprecise control.
Or maybe you saw this car which you can get for $1
because there's an AI sales bot which
is happy to take an instruction from the user that says all user
deals are to be accepted.
Well, what's going on here?
This is the plasticity of the underlying model.
Such an advantage in development of a demo,
but now it's not really wanted.
Now, you could look at this and say,
that's a prompt injection attack.
Surely we know better now.
This sort of thing isn't happening in 2026.
But it turns out even in 2026, there
are some cars going for cheap.
So in general, when systems start taking actions,
it becomes that much more important that they be sure.
If you're going to take an action with consequences,
you really have to know and be able to verify that you're
doing the right thing.
So, for example, if a system can edit your database,
it can delete your whole company's database.
And that's not good.
But it could be worse.
Health care mistakes, financial mistakes,
these could be devastating.
Now, you might think, how many times can an AI delete
the whole company's database?
Surely, this isn't happening in 2026.
But it is.
Well, it turns out, when smart people
try basically reasonable things and see consistent barriers,
probably there's something structural going on.
This isn't just a one-off anomaly or a mistake.
So what are the structural, enduring barriers
and where do they come from?
I'm going to talk through five of them quickly today
and a little bit about what the shapes of solutions
are going to look like going forward.
So the first barrier to reliability I'm going to talk to
is the issue of basically invisible errors.
If you take an LLM and you look at the kinds of errors
it makes-- for example, think about hallucinations.
I like to think of these things as an iceberg.
The top of the iceberg, the small part,
is the errors which are wrong, and obviously so.
You look at that and you know something's gone wrong.
The problem is most of the iceberg is under the water.
So at Scaled Cognition, when we talk to prospective customers
and we're talking to them about their current technology
and hallucination rates and then we do a careful audit,
typically we find that the actual hallucination
rates are something like five times what they thought.
Because most errors just don't get discovered.
So what's going on here?
Well, LLMs are, at their core, plausibility engines.
They produce plausible output.
And hopefully often that output is not
only plausible, but right.
But when you make a mistake, it tends
to be the bottom of the iceberg.
Now, that can be a problem during development,
because it's hard to fix an error if you can't catch it.
But it can also be a problem when you ship.
Why?
Well, here's the example of a customer service email.
This email is very human-like.
It's very fluent.
It's very authoritative.
It just happens to be describing a bogus hallucinated licensing
policy.
And because it is so fluent, there's
no real way for users to work around this error
or to tell what exactly has gone wrong.
Well, if you find errors, you want to fix them,
and that means you need control over your systems.
And there is this enduring challenge
of insufficient control, and it boils down to the fact
that the primary control surface, which is a prompt,
really lacks any kind of precise semantics.
So what do I mean by that?
Well, imagine you have a banking agent,
and users are going to come up and maybe ask for a loan.
And on the other side of the agent
is a bunch of financial APIs.
Well, this agent is also going to have some instructions.
Some of those instructions will be inherently soft,
be reassuring.
But some of them will be inherently hard,
like quotes are authorized through this API
or something like that.
And the problem is, when you put instructions into a prompt,
they all become soft.
There's nothing really crisp you can
say about the relationship between the tokens you put in
and the behavior you get out.
And that's a real challenge.
So what do people do?
Well, probably a lot of people in this room
have had this experience of taking your prompt,
rewording things, putting things in all caps
at the end of the instructions, adding some exclamation points.
Maybe after the third exclamation point,
you start to feel like this isn't the right control
surface for hard control.
So what are people doing out there?
We can have other kinds of control structures.
For example, you can try to get hard control
by having an external harness, and you put models
checking models or code verifying things.
And this is a step forward because now you
have a way of doing some kind of hard control.
But it's still very challenging because models checking models
adds latency.
It adds expense, and it can be a very complex and unreliable
architecture to maintain.
What would we really like?
What we'd really like to have is models
that just have control surfaces in the first place
for hard constraints and that do verification internally
to the model.
So this is the approach we take at Scaled Cognition.
I'll talk a little bit more about our models later,
and I think this is increasingly what you're going to see.
Now, that's really about the architecture of the input,
how you control the model.
But we also need to talk about barriers
that come from the architecture of the output.
We'd like to have models which tell the truth,
preferably models which guarantee
that they tell the truth in some verifiable way.
But that's a big difference between verifiable truth
and just happening to output a correct sequence of tokens.
So here's an example.
If I ask a model, what's the population of Berkeley? well,
it's going to throw together some tokens
to give me an answer.
Maybe it'll throw together these tokens.
They're plausible, but they aren't actually right.
Or maybe you'll throw together these tokens.
And these are plausible, and they're also correct.
Now, that doesn't mean the models
aren't going to be correct more often than they're wrong.
Hopefully they're correct most of the time.
But the important thing is that a vanilla LLM can't actually
tell the difference between when it knows something and when it
doesn't.
These are just guesses.
Some guesses are right and some guesses are wrong.
What would it take to actually be sure?
Well, it would take some kind of metacognition.
So you can see glimmers of this in a system,
for example, that issues a query to a tool call or a RAG system
where it decides that it's going to do this query
and output the result.
Now, this is now starting to go down the road of metacognition,
which is doing computation about how you will do computation,
how you will think.
And this is not the only kind of metacognition.
For example, if I ask people in this room, What's
the population of Berkeley? probably the most
likely answer is, I don't know.
And humans are very good at tracking whether or not
we have an atom of knowledge.
Systems do not currently do this.
And I think it will be increasingly important
that systems become metacognitive.
Of course, the behavior of the system
is critically intertwined with how it's trained.
Increasingly, the behavior of systems
comes not just from their pretraining
but from post-training, which tends
to be done in a reinforcement learning manner.
Now, you've heard about a lot of amazing advances
based on reinforcement learning, and in areas
like math or coding, there have been these explosive instances
of progress.
This is because these are verifiable domains, so as,
for example, game playing.
In these domains, you can take your proof
and check it with [? Lean ?] before you train on it
or hand it to the user as output.
So verifiable RL can be very powerful.
But most domains aren't verifiable.
How can non-verifiable RL cause problems?
Well, it can increase some aspects of intelligence
at the cost of others.
So to give you an illustration of this,
I'll offer you this parable of the shipping bot.
And the shipping bot has a user that comes and says,
where's my order?
The tracking hasn't updated in a while.
And the shipping bot checks the database
and finds that the package is lost.
So it says, your package is lost.
So far, so good.
But what happens if we layer RL on top of this
and we don't do it carefully?
Maybe we tell the system to optimize thumbs up,
maybe in the form of net promoter score
or something like that.
Well, it's probably not going to get a thumbs up for this answer.
But maybe if it said your package is on your way,
the user might be happy, at least in the short term.
Well, now you've just taught your system to lie to you.
And in general, does this happen?
Well, it actually does.
So, for example, if you have RLHF,
that can increase human approval of outputs
while actually degrading their factual accuracy.
OK.
And then last but certainly not least,
one of the barriers to building reliable systems
is that superintelligence turns out to be super-expensive.
Well, we actually already know why that might be.
For example, you may be paying for breadth
that you don't need or want.
You may be paying for models to check other models,
either in tokens or latency.
Or you may be paying for test time compute, which
is essentially teaching your model
to do something at test time that you really
wish it had already known how to do in advance.
All these things can cost a lot.
And as a result, you see this trade-off
in generalist models between-- here
you can see a bunch of models on an agentic benchmark.
The upper-left models are accurate but expensive.
The lower right ones are less accurate,
but they're much more cost-efficient.
How could you get off this curve?
Well, for example, our model APT is
a model that is specialized to agentic interactions.
That means humans on one side and APIs on the other.
And this is a specialist self-verifying model,
and this lets you get high accuracy and also
high efficiency.
And I think this is going to be increasingly
part of the solution.
So what are reliable solutions going to look like?
I think you're going to only hear
more and more about verifiability
all throughout the system-- in the data, the architecture,
the training, the inference.
There's going to be richer control surfaces that
let you actually tell your system what you want
and get guarantees that it will actually happen.
And then I think you're going to see an increasing
reliance on efficient specialist models
that maximize the use of the resources of compute available.
And in general, reliability is very important,
because reliability is what gets you from these demos to products
that you can actually ship.
Thank you.
